item.title: Financial Returns, Sentiment and Market Volatility: A Dynamic Assessment
item.description:
Journal of Forecasting ｜ 综合分 35.0 ｜ 上线 2026-11-24（0 天前） · 在线 2026-11-23

ABSTRACT This paper investigates the relationship between sentiment and financial market activity in Italy using the Social Mood on Economy Index (SMEI), a daily sentiment indicator produced by the Italian National Statistical Institute (ISTAT) from the textual analysis of Twitter (X) messages. We examine the dynamic interactions among SMEI, FTSE‐MIB returns and market volatility within a trivariate Vector Autoregressive framework. Particular attention is devoted to the structural changes induced by the COVID‐19 pandemic.The analysis is conducted separately for the pre‐ and post‐COVID‐19 periods and is complemented by rolling‐window causality analysis and out‐of‐sample forecasting exercises. The results indicate that before the pandemic, market volatility is the only variable significantly affected by lagged information from the other variables. During and after the pandemic, the relationships become substantially stronger and more interconnected: lagged volatility Granger‐causes both sentiment and returns, lagged returns affect volatility and sentiment itself acquires predictive content for volatility. Out‐of‐sample forecast comparisons further show that sentiment information improves forecasts of market volatility, whereas its contribution to forecasting returns remains limited. Overall, the findings suggest that social media–based measures of economic mood provide valuable information for understanding and forecasting market volatility, particularly during periods characterised by elevated uncertainty and rapidly changing expectations.

item.title: Deep Tangency Portfolio
item.description:
Management Science ｜ 综合分 42.9 ｜ 上线 2026-11-23（1 天前）

We develop a deep learning framework to directly estimate tangency portfolio weights by augmenting benchmark factors with a long-short deep factor derived from high-dimensional characteristics. Guided by a Sharpe ratio maximization objective, the deep factor plays two key roles: (i) providing a natural hedge against benchmark risks and (ii) capturing multimarket signals to enhance the performance of the benchmark. In an empirical application to U.S. corporate bonds using 132 firm-level bond, equity, and option characteristics, the deep factor achieves an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio exceeding one, and the deep tangency portfolio benchmarked against the market factor yields a Sharpe ratio over two, outperforming portfolios spanned by common observable or latent factors. These results demonstrate that bond risk signals are fundamentally dense, requiring the nonlinear integration of multimarket information to span the efficient frontier. item.title: Learning from a Biased Sample
item.description:
Management Science ｜ 综合分 38.3 ｜ 上线 2026-11-23（1 天前）

The empirical risk minimization approach to data-driven decision making requires access to training data drawn under the same conditions as those that will be faced when the decision rule is deployed. However, we may be concerned that our training sample is biased in the sense that some groups (characterized by either observable or unobservable attributes) may be under- or over-represented relative to the general population; and in this setting, empirical risk minimization over the training set may fail to yield rules that perform well at deployment. We propose a model of sampling bias called conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling, where observed covariates can affect the probability of sample selection arbitrarily much but the amount of unexplained variation in the probability of sample selection is bounded by a constant factor. Applying the distributionally robust optimization framework, we propose a method for learning a decision rule that minimizes the worst-case risk incurred under a family of test distributions that can generate the training distribution under conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling. We apply a result of Rockafellar and Uryasev to show that this problem is equivalent to an augmented convex risk minimization problem. We give statistical guarantees for learning a model that is robust to sampling bias via the method of sieves, and propose a deep learning algorithm whose loss function captures our robust learning target. We empirically validate our proposed method in a case study on prediction of mental health scores from health survey data and a case study on intensive care unit length-of-stay prediction. This paper was accepted by Vivek Farias, data science. Funding: This research was supported by NSF grant SES-2242876. RS is further supported by a NSF GRFP under grant DGE-1656518, a Stanford Data Science PhD Fellowship, and a Stanford Diversifying Academia Recruiting Excellence (DARE) Fellowship. item.title: Optimal Incentive Design for Decentralized Dynamic Matching Markets
item.description:
Management Science ｜ 综合分 38.3 ｜ 上线 2026-11-23（1 天前）

In decentralized dynamic matching markets, agents can benefit from sharing resources, but they will collaborate only if properly incentivized. Motivated by applications such as multihospital kidney exchanges and job-hunting markets, this paper proposes novel monetary and nonmonetary mechanisms to incentivize collaboration in such decentralized dynamic markets. We study a model in which multiple self-interested agents manage local multiway dynamic matching problems. Jobs of different types arrive stochastically at each agent, expire after a limited time, and yield rewards when matched. An agent’s job backlog and actions are the agent’s private information, and each agent aims to maximize its long-run average matching reward. We design simple mechanisms that incentivize agents to submit all jobs upon arrival, thereby enabling centralized matching. Our first mechanism, the marginal-value (MV) mechanism, reimburses agents based on the MV of their submitted jobs. This can be implemented in a nonmonetary way by randomly selecting an agent (with a specified probability) to perform a match and collect the associated matching reward. We show that under the MV mechanism, full job submission constitutes an approximate Nash equilibrium—that is, the gain from unilateral deviation vanishes as the number of agents grows. To further eliminate incentives for deviation, we propose a refined mechanism, the MV-plus-credit (MVC) mechanism, and show that, when the number of agents exceeds a constant threshold, full job submission constitutes a stronger oblivious equilibrium. Numerical experiments based on kidney exchange data demonstrate that the gains from deviation under our mechanisms are small even in moderately sized markets. This paper was accepted by Peng Sun, optimization and decision analytics. Funding: J. item.title: Proximity-Based Delivery Policies: Efficiency, Coverage, and Fairness
item.description:
Management Science ｜ 综合分 38.3 ｜ 上线 2026-11-23（1 天前）

The growing demand for rapid food and grocery delivery has prompted many restaurants and retailers to develop their own on-demand delivery services. Although hiring additional couriers can expand delivery capacity, it is often prohibitively costly. As a cost-effective alternative, we propose a proximity-based delivery (PBD) policy that prioritizes the delivery of orders from customers located closer to the vendor, in contrast to the traditional first-come-first-served (FCFS) approach. We show that PBD can substantially reduce average delivery delays without requiring additional couriers; however, it may raise fairness concerns, because distant customers experience longer wait times, potentially shrinking market coverage and exacerbating service disparities. To address this issue, we introduce an incentive-compatible PBD (IP) policy, where nearby customers are incentivized to pay for priority, whereas distant customers receive compensation to offset longer delays. We demonstrate that this mechanism can restore fairness to levels comparable to FCFS while preserving efficiency, expanding market demand, and enhancing consumer surplus, particularly in moderately dense markets with moderately delay-sensitive customers. We further show that vendors can enhance these benefits through optimal pricing and benefit from less extreme staffing adjustments due to a “pull-to-center” effect. Our findings highlight the operational, economic, and ethical dimensions of proximity-based delivery, and offer a practical framework for balancing speed, profitability, consumer welfare, and equity. Finally, we conduct a mini case study using empirical data to demonstrate the real-world applicability of our approach. This paper was accepted by Jeannette Song, operations management. Funding: Z. item.title: Stockouts and the Success of New Products
item.description:
Management Science ｜ 综合分 37.6 ｜ 上线 2026-11-23（1 天前）

We investigate how stockouts of existing products influence the success of new product introductions. Our findings reveal that stockouts on incumbent items at the time a new product is launched are associated with higher sales of the new product for at least six months. This positive spillover is specific to new products and is most potent at the start of the product life cycle. To establish causality, we use instrumental variables based on historical stockouts and contemporaneous stockouts in other stores. Analysis of individual-level transaction data corroborates a trial-and-adoption mechanism: Stockouts of existing items prompt consumers to trial the new product, leading to increased repeat purchasing. By identifying inventory as a driver of product trial, this research highlights the importance of strategically timing new product launches and documents a previously unrecognized tradeoff for inventory policies. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02602 .

item.title: Collateral Demand in Wholesale Funding Markets
item.description:
Review of Financial Studies ｜ 综合分 35.6 ｜ 上线 2026-11-23（1 天前）

Abstract Repo markets are systemically important funding markets, but are also used by firms to obtain the assets provided as collateral. We build and structurally estimate a model of trade between heterogeneous firms in the sterling gilt repo market, and show that this collateral demand depresses repo market activity and can impede the transmission of monetary policy. We quantify how well-designed central bank repo facilities can improve outcomes: if the central bank were to lend out the assets on its balance sheet following quantitative easing, transmission and total firm surplus would improve by 20% and 38%, respectively.

item.title: Information Design with Supplemental Investment
item.description:
Management Science ｜ 综合分 32.9 ｜ 上线 2026-11-23（1 天前）

This paper features a setting with two-dimensional information asymmetry on a firm’s fundamental (good or bad type) and the nature of its supplemental investment (improving upside potential, or mitigating downside risk). We examine the firm’s optimal design of the information system when the system can only address the dimension of fundamental. We show that, with only single-dimensional information asymmetry regarding the firm’s fundamental, greater informativeness on the firm’s fundamental type always improves efficiency. However, with two-dimensional information asymmetry, increasing informativeness about firm fundamental no longer guarantees higher efficiency and can be detrimental. The optimal information system trades off reducing information asymmetry and preserving firms’ incentives to invest, and it could be uninformative or optimistically biased, depending on the level of credit risk, which in our setting is higher when supplemental investment is more likely to improve upside rather than protect downside. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00524 .

Abstract We introduce CHILE, an asset-pricing framework with asymmetric information, general utility functions, and arbitrary payoffs. It features a large economy (LE) with continuous-and-heterogeneous information (CHI). The defining feature of this information structure is that the total amount of information stays finite as the economy grows large. We use the framework to study how concentration—the presence of market participants of different sizes—affects market quality, namely liquidity and information efficiency. Greater concentration proves a double-edged sword: it raises liquidity but harms information efficiency. (JEL D01, D53, D82, E19, G12, G14)

item.title: Informal Redistribution Through Work
item.description:
Econometrica ｜ 综合分 33.9 ｜ 上线 2026-11-19（2 天前） · 在线 2026-01-01

We investigate work as informal redistribution, leveraging field experiments and firm‐level survey data from Kampala, Uganda. Employers and workers consistently choose redistribution through work over cash transfers, revealing a willingness to pay for work. By randomizing work tasks—some designed to have zero marginal product—we find that production value does not explain these choices: employers pay for zero‐value work. These patterns are also inconsistent with other relational benefits, such as social image concerns or networking. Instead, motivations are normative. Experimental evidence reveals an internalized norm for redistribution through work rooted in incentive arguments on the demand side—as employers stop requiring work only when workers have verifiable emergencies—and in reciprocity and dignity from earning on the supply side. The norm shapes both the organization and measurement of production: failing to account for redistribution through work makes firms appear significantly larger and less productive than they are.

item.title: Comment on ‘Selection and Comparative Advantage in Technology Adoption’ by Tavneet Suri
item.description:
Econometrica ｜ 综合分 41.4 ｜ 上线 2026-11-19（1 天前） · 在线 2026-01-01

This paper illustrates and addresses weak identification in the correlated random coefficient (CRC) model that Suri (2011) uses to study agricultural technology adoption. Using the publicly available data set, which differs slightly from the version used in Suri (2011), we obtain different point estimates for the paper's main CRC model. To understand why these differences are as large as they are, we recast the CRC model as a more general random coefficient model in which the returns to hybrid adoption are restricted to be linear in comparative advantage. This reveals that the key structural parameter in the CRC model ( ϕ ), which governs the relationship between baseline productivity and the returns to adoption, is prone to a weak‐identification problem. We then propose a procedure to conduct weak‐identification robust inference on ϕ using test inversion. Our weak‐identification robust confidence intervals contain the original Suri (2011) point estimates, which suggests that the difference in results may be attributable to a combination of minor data differences and weak identification.

item.title: Sample Range as Subjective Variability and Implications for Experience-Based Decision Making
item.description:
Management Science ｜ 综合分 38.6 ｜ 上线 2026-11-19（1 天前）

Variance and standard deviation are common metrics of statistical variability in the management and decision-making literature. In everyday contexts, however, information about sample range prevails. Range is arguably easier to comprehend and compute than variance, yet it often yields equivalent judgments about variability. Hence, we reason that decision makers often rely on range to judge variability. We test this hypothesis across four behavioral experiments (total n = 1,093). When comparing the variability of two number sets, decision makers predominantly based their judgments on sample range rather than sample variance when the two metrics disagree (experiment 1). Sample range tends to increase with sample size, whereas sample variance does not. Consistent with the range as variability hypothesis, decision makers perceived distributions as more variable after observing larger samples (experiment 2). This perceived variability, in turn, influenced risky decisions, as larger sample sizes led to decreased valuations of uncertain rewards for risk-averse decision makers (experiment 3). In further support of the hypothesis, when asked to mentally simulate new samples from a previously experienced distribution, participants generated more numbers within the observed range and fewer numbers outside of it than the true distribution implies (experiment 4). To model the data, we propose a “cognitive fence” idea as a potential psychological explanation for how experience shapes subjective variability. We conclude by discussing implications for research on overconfidence, distributional learning, risk perception, and communication. This paper was accepted by Jack Soll, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05050 .

item.title: The Social Learning Barrier
item.description:
Econometrica ｜ 综合分 36.8 ｜ 上线 2026-11-19（1 天前） · 在线 2026-01-01

Long‐lived agents interact repeatedly in a social network. In each period, each agent observes a private signal, chooses an action, and then observes the actions of her neighbors. We show that the learning rate of the slowest‐learning agent is capped by a constant that depends only on the distribution of the most informative private signal, but not on the number of agents, the network structure, correlations between the private signals, or the agents' strategies. For equilibrium learning with rational agents, the same result bounds the learning rate of every agent in any equilibrium under a broad class of conditions. The result is driven by an information‐theoretic tradeoff between optimal action choices and information revelation.

item.title: Why Are the Wealthiest so Wealthy? New Longitudinal Empirical Evidence and Implications for Theories of Wealth Inequality
item.description:
Econometrica ｜ 综合分 36.8 ｜ 上线 2026-11-19（1 天前） · 在线 2026-01-01

We study the lifecycle dynamics of wealth inequality using 1993–2019 Norwegian administrative panel data on wealth and income. Employing a novel budget‐constraint approach, we decompose the excess wealth of the top 0.1% households relative to the median between ages 45 and 64 into higher saving rates (36%), inheritances (31%), returns (28%), and labor income (5%). One‐quarter of the wealthiest—the “New Money”—start with negative wealth on average but accumulate rapidly through high labor income and exceptionally high saving rates and returns. The “Old Money” inherit substantial wealth and grow it through above‐average though more modest saving and returns. We use these dynamic facts to evaluate five standard wealth inequality models. Although these models match cross‐sectional wealth concentration, they fail to reproduce the distinct dynamics of New and Old Money. A heterogeneous entrepreneurship model with decreasing returns to scale technology and nonhomothetic preferences is consistent with the observed dynamics.

item.description:

Multivariate linear regression and randomization‐based inference are two essential methods in statistics and econometrics. Nevertheless, the problem of producing a randomized test for the value of a single regression coefficient that is exactly valid when errors are exchangeable, and which is asymptotically valid for the best linear predictor, has remained elusive. In this paper, we produce a test that is exactly valid with exchangeable errors and which allows for general covariate designs; covariates may be continuous as well as discrete and may be correlated. The test is asymptotically valid when the errors are not exchangeable, in particular in the presence of conditional heteroskedasticity.

item.description:

I develop a new method for estimating production functions with labor‐augmenting technology and apply it to markup estimation. ABSTRACT Accurate carbon price forecasts support allowance trading, compliance planning and market supervision. This study examines whether two temporal representations of the same carbon price series—the original chronological sequence (horizontal dimension) and five weekday‐structured subsequences (vertical dimension) obtained by regrouping Monday‐to‐Friday observations—contain complementary predictive information. Both representations are modeled within a common decomposition‐reconstruction‐forecasting framework: Dynamic time warping (DTW) diagnoses the correspondence between them, complete ensemble empirical mode decomposition with adaptive noise (CEEMDAN) and sample entropy (SE) decompose and reconstruct each series, and a leaky‐integrator echo state network (LiESN) generates the forecasts. Abstract People persist in mistaken beliefs even in settings with high stakes, abundant data, and repeated opportunities to learn—settings where standard arguments imply they should correct their errors. item.description:

ABSTRACT This study proposes a time‐varying structural approximate dynamic factor (TVS‐ADF) model by extending the approximate dynamic factor (ADF) model in state‐space form. The TVS‐ADF model considers time‐varying coefficients and a time‐varying variance–covariance matrix of its innovation terms to capture complex economic dynamics. We propose the identification scheme of the common factors in the TVS‐ADF model and derive the identification theory. We also propose an effective Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to estimate the TVS‐ADF model. To avoid the overparameterization caused by the time‐varying characteristics of the TVS‐ADF model, we include the shrinkage and sparsification approaches in the MCMC algorithm. Extensive simulation experiments and empirical applications demonstrate the outstanding performance of the TVS‐ADF model.

item.title: Two-stage least squares with treatment-covariate interactions for treatment effect heterogeneity
item.description:
Journal of Econometrics ｜ 综合分 32.1 ｜ 上线 2026-11-04（5 天前） · 在线 2026-11-01

Treatment effect heterogeneity with respect to covariates is common in instrumental variable (IV) analyses. An intuitive approach, which we call the interacted two-stage least squares (2sls), is to regress the outcome on the treatment, covariates, and treatment-covariate interactions, using the IV, covariates, and IV-covariate interactions as instruments. We clarify the causal interpretation of the interacted 2sls under the local average treatment effect (LATE) framework when the IV is valid conditional on the covariates. Our main findings are twofold. First, we show that the coefficients on the treatment-covariate interactions from the interacted 2sls identify treatment effect heterogeneity with respect to covariates among compliers for any outcome-generating process if and only if the product of the IV propensity score and the covariates is linear in the covariates, a requirement we call the linear IV-covariate interactions condition. Second, when the covariate vector has dimension K and includes a constant term, we show that the linear IV-covariate interactions condition requires the IV propensity score to take at most K distinct values. The condition holds when (a) the covariates take exactly K distinct values, or (b) the IV is randomly assigned independently of the covariates, but is restrictive beyond these cases. These results underscore the difficulty of interpreting regression coefficients from specifications with treatment-covariate interactions when the covariates are not saturated and the IV is not unconditionally randomized, absent correct specification of the outcome model. We then connect these results to the literature on LATE estimation, and show that under the linear IV-covariate interactions condition, the interacted 2sls with covariates demeaned by their complier means recovers the LATE as a single coefficient.

ABSTRACT We reinvestigate Anderson, Reeb, and Zhao's findings that informed short selling is unique to family firms and driven by information leakage from internal disputes. Using the same firm sample and more comprehensive short‐selling data, we find that short selling predicts future returns in both family and nonfamily firms. We also find no significant difference in abnormal short selling before negative earnings announcements. In extended sample periods, short selling continues to predict returns for nonfamily firms under both ownership‐based and familial‐link definitions. Overall, our evidence suggests that short sellers are broadly informed and that family firms are not uniquely vulnerable.

item.title: The effect of extreme wildfire exposure on energy poverty: Evidence from Australia's Black Saturday bushfires
item.description:
American Journal of Agricultural Economics ｜ 综合分 36.4 ｜ 上线 2026-11-04（1 天前）

Abstract This study assesses the effects of the 2009 Black Saturday Bushfires (BSB), which primarily occurred in rural regions of Victoria and represent the deadliest bushfire event in Australia's history, on household energy poverty. Using a linear panel event‐study, an entropy‐balanced event‐study, and a staggered difference‐in‐differences (DiD) design, applied to matched longitudinal household and geographical data, our results suggest a significant increase in the likelihood of experiencing energy poverty among households residing within 15 km of wildfire areas. Specifically, we find that for households directly affected by the fires, the likelihood of being in energy poverty increases by 9.9–11.3 percentage points in 2010 and by 13.2–16.7 percentage points in 2011 across specifications, compared to 2005–2007, which is the reference period. We find that the data are statistically consistent with life satisfaction, perceived safety and quality of life fully mediating the effect of BSB exposure on energy poverty in 2010, and with perceived safety fully mediating the relationship in 2011. We also find that adopting longer‐term financial planning mitigated the adverse effects of BSB exposure on energy poverty.

item.title: Are dairy cows replaced too early? Evidence from a structural model and cow‐level data
item.description:
American Journal of Agricultural Economics ｜ 综合分 33.6 ｜ 上线 2026-11-04（1 天前）

Abstract In past analyses of animal replacement decisions, studies have claimed that dairy farms often replace dairy cows too early to be maximizing profits. I estimate a structural model of asset replacement to determine the motives behind early replacement of dairy cows. I specifically test whether the costs from premature removal, an event where cows are removed off‐schedule due to health problems, explain replacement ages on dairy farms that are considered by previous studies to be unprofitable. Using data from over 1000 Wisconsin dairy farms, I find that a cow prematurely leaving the herd costs $2300 per removal, totaling $75 million in lost profit over the sample period. This cost is larger than what has been previously assumed, especially for dairies with less than 200 cows, suggesting that replacement rates appear unprofitable because previous analyses underestimated these costs. Dairy farms may benefit from prioritizing cow longevity and health over productivity to both cut costs and address environmental externalities from dairy. These results highlight the economic damages from poor cattle health on US dairy farms and the extent to which there may be cost savings from increasing cattle resilience to conditions that cause unexpected removal.

item.title: Why Do Union Jobs Pay More? New Evidence from Matched Employer-Employee Data
item.description:
The Quarterly Journal of Economics ｜ 综合分 38.5 ｜ 上线 2026-11-03（3 天前） · 在线 2026-11-05

Abstract We use Canadian matched employer-employee data to assess the sources of the union pay premium. After controlling for worker heterogeneity using the two-way fixed effects approach of Abowd, Kramarz, and Margolis (AKM), we find that unionized firms pay about 15 log points more than non-unionized firms. Forty percent of this gap is linked to productivity differences between unionized and non-unionized firms as measured by value added per worker. The remaining gap reflects unions’ ability to extract more rents for workers. Our estimates imply that unions raise pay among unionized workers by around 9 log points, with considerable heterogeneity by industry and firm birth cohorts. The union effect grows to about 11 log points in an extension of the AKM approach where unions also affect the returns to unobservable worker characteristics.
